thread.title: Dialog Semiconductor On The Clock - Dialog Semiconductor Plc (OTCMKTS:DLGNF)

author: Stephen Simpson, CFA
title: Dialog Semiconductor On The Clock - Dialog Semiconductor Plc (OTCMKTS:DLGNF)
text:
A year ago, the debate around Dialog Semiconductor ( OTCPK:DLGNF ) was whether or not there was any substance to bearish rumors and predictions that Apple ( AAPL ) was working on its own power management integrated circuits (or PMICs) and would use them to replace Dialog’s chips in its iPhones and other products. With Apple having since done exactly that (although not completely), now the debate is how far the substitutions will go and what Dialog can do to preserve and rebuild its business absent contributions from Apple that have historically made up 70% or more of revenue (and high-margin revenue at that).
Both Dialog and Synaptics ( SYNA ) have confirmed that they’re discussing a merger; while Synaptics has been a frequent-flier on sell-side “likely to be bought” charts, and there would be potential synergies in such a deal, Dialog’s iffy history in M&A doesn’t lend a lot of confidence. The good news, such as it is, though, is that the market is already pricing in a very dire outlook for this beaten-up chip company.
Dialog In Limbo … How Low Will Apple Go? Not only did Apple and Dialog confirm back in December of 2017 that Apple had an internal PMIC effort underway (which really wasn’t a secret), but Apple has moved quicker than expected in bringing its own PMICs into play with its iPhones. For the iPhones coming out in the second half of this year, Apple will be in-sourcing the PMICs for one of three, with Dialog-provided PMICs for the other two and sub-PMICs for all three. Dialog has also, thus far, maintained its PMIC business with the iPad and other Apple products.
What happens from here is clearly a huge question for Dialog; Apple represents virtually all of Dialog’s Mobile business (which was 72% of Q1’18 revenue and 77% of 2017 revenue), and this is far and away the biggest source of Dialog’s profits. While Apple is being cautious with the introduction of its first primary PMICs, I would expect Apple to look to replace Dialog in other primary sockets over the next year or two, potentially blowing a huge hole in Dialog’s business that ongoing sub-PMIC orders will do little to salvage.
Dialog doesn’t really have any good choices here. While management continues to talk about working with other smartphone OEMs, the track record is what it is, and the company has had no success or traction working with other customers. What’s more, unless Dialog wants to just walk away from Apple’s business entirely, there are still ongoing R&D and SG&A needs to keep this business going.
Is Synaptics The Right Answer? It’s no surprise that Dialog is looking to M&A to rebuild its future. The company has just over $500 million in cash, cash flow that could support debt for an accretive acquisition, as well as equity currency that still has some value. To that end, both Synaptics and Dialog have acknowledged they’re in merger discussions, roughly a week after a report from Bloomberg that Synaptics had rejected a $59/share bid.
Synaptics is an interesting choice. The business is in transition, with a steady decline in quarterly revenue since 2017, but with some promising exposures to growth markets like OLED, auto infotainment, and IoT. Gross margins are not great (and have been sliding for years), and likewise with operating margins. And yet, Synaptics has been a popular name on “chip companies likely to get bought out” due to the above-average return potential of driving better gross margins and stripping operating costs out of the business.
What’s more, there are potential operational synergies with Dialog as well. Synaptics’ specialty is in interface solutions, and these products consume significant amounts of power. Dialog’s specialty is in power management and recently (late 2017) acquired Silego – a company that specializes in configurable mixed-signal integrated circuits (or CMICs) that combine multiple functions on a single chip.
I don’t doubt that acquiring Synaptics could create some meaningful design, revenue, and profit synergies for Dialog, but I do question whether management can execute on that potential. Thus far, Dialog’s track record of identifying good deals, paying reasonable prices, getting the deal done, and successfully leveraging the acquired property is mixed at best. Given the size of Synaptics, a failure to maximize the value of this deal would be a devastating blow.
The Opportunity Modeling Dialog is very difficult right now, as there’s really no way to know whether Apple will gradually replace their remaining PMIC business with internally-sourced chips, quickly switch over to their own chips, or hold the line. I’m expecting severe erosion at this point, as I believe Dialog could keep the sub-PMIC business for a while, but I think the main PMIC business is destined to disappear.
The good news, if you can call it that, is that there’s really very little priced into the shares right now. If I strip out all of the expected Mobile revenue for 2018 and use a high single-digit EBIT margin assumption for what remains, a 2x revenue multiple (which is reasonable for that level of margin) would give me a fair value about 5% above Dialog’s current price. And remember, the Mobile/Apple business isn’t going to zero this year, and Dialog's PMIC technology does have other potential applications (like IoT).
Clearly, a deal for Synaptics would meaningfully alter the value equation, and that too is tough to model, given no real clarity on price or deal composition. Even so, I am comfortable with the general idea that the market is already pricing in a very gloomy future for Dialog.
The Bottom Line Stocks rarely outperform just because they’re cheap. Dialog still has a viable business outside of Mobile/PMICs, but management has a bad track record with M&A (missing out on Atmel and AMS AG ( OTCPK:AMSSY ), paying a lot for Silego), and making a Synaptics deal work is not going to be a simple task. While I do think that the price/valuation on Dialog looks extremely low, and there is value in the non-Mobile operations, the uncertainty is off the charts, and a great deal of the company’s future value now lies with the outcome of these negotiations with Synaptics.
